# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and definition

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterised by delayed opacification of the distal coronary vasculature in the absence of significant epicardial stenosis. It was first described in 1972, when Tambe, Demany, Zimmerman and Mascarenhas reported angina pectoris and slow flow velocity of dye in coronary arteries as a new angiographic finding. More than four decades later, it remains incompletely understood. The CSFP is an angiographic entity characterized by delayed progression of the injected contrast medium through the coronary tree; it is a frequent finding, typically observed in patients presenting with acute coronary syndromes, and although well known to interventional cardiologists for approximately four decades, the pathogenic mechanisms remain unclear. The condition has also been termed "cardiac syndrome Y," and it is a relatively poorly understood microvascular coronary artery disorder caused by increased microvascular coronary artery resistance to flow that may result in myocardial infarction at rest in young individuals.

Beltrame and colleagues helped establish CSFP as a distinct disorder. In their case-control study, the coronary slow flow phenomenon was characterised by delayed distal vessel opacification in the absence of significant epicardial coronary disease, and it was speculated to be a new disease entity characterised by acute but recurrent perturbations of microvascular function.

## Diagnosis and quantification

Diagnosis rests on objective angiographic quantification of coronary flow. The corrected TIMI frame count (CTFC) is the number of cine frames required for dye to first reach standardized distal coronary landmarks, and it is an objective and quantitative index of coronary blood flow. The method was introduced by Gibson and colleagues, who showed that the left anterior descending coronary artery TIMI frame count was 1.7 times longer than the mean of the right and circumflex counts, so the longer LAD counts were corrected by dividing by 1.7 to derive the corrected TIMI frame count. A correlation with adverse outcomes exists, as patients who died in the hospital had a higher CTFC (slower flow) than survivors. Importantly, primary CSFP must be distinguished from secondary causes. Primary CSFP should be distinguished from delayed contrast progression in the context of coronary reperfusion therapy or other "secondary" causes including coronary artery ectasia, coronary artery spasm, valvular heart disease, or connective tissue disorders.

## Epidemiology and clinical presentation

CSFP is more common than often appreciated. Coronary slow flow, also known as cardiac syndrome Y, is characterised by angiographically normal or near-normal coronary arteries with delayed opacification of the distal vasculature; it has clinical implications such as angina, acute coronary syndrome and sudden death, with a prevalence ranging from 1–5% of coronary angiograms and a predilection for young male smokers. In a large series, CSFP was identified in 5.5% of subjects referred for angiography and was associated with male sex and obesity. The clinical burden is considerable: over 80% of patients experience recurrent chest pain, resulting in considerable impairment in quality of life. A wide presentation is recognised, since CSFP has a diverse presentation from mild chest discomfort to ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction, can have severe morbidity and mortality implications, and can significantly hamper quality of life. Concerningly, CSFP has been reported in patients presenting with anginal chest pain and recurrent syncope, with multiple episodes of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia and increased QTc dispersion, linking the phenomenon to a risk of malignant arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death.

## Pathophysiology

Several mechanisms have been proposed. Endothelial dysfunction is central; CSFP is thought to reflect endothelial dysfunction, with inflammation, atherosclerosis, hematological disorders, and structural components also contributing, though the exact cause is still not fully understood. Histopathological studies support a small-vessel substrate. Mosseri and colleagues studied patients with angina and patent large arteries and found that during coronary angiography these patients had significantly reduced flow velocity of angiographic contrast medium compared with a control group, providing histologic evidence for small-vessel disease. Earlier work demonstrated small vessel thickening with luminal narrowing and ultrastructural abnormalities, suggesting that fibromuscular hyperplasia and medial hypertrophy lead to functional obstruction.

Invasive haemodynamic studies clarified the functional substrate. Beltrame and colleagues found that the corrected TIMI frame count remained delayed compared with control subjects, and resting coronary sinus oxygen saturation was low, reflecting increased basal coronary vasomotor tone. An inflammatory contribution is also supported, since increased plasma C-reactive protein and interleukin-6 concentrations have been demonstrated in patients with slow coronary flow.

## Management

No therapy is firmly established, but several agents show benefit. The strongest evidence comes from a randomised trial of the calcium T-channel blocker mibefradil, in which mibefradil significantly reduced total angina frequency by 56%, prolonged episodes by 74%, and nitrate consumption by 59%, and improved physical quality of life, supporting a microspastic pathogenesis of the CSFP. Oral dipyridamole has also been used successfully, and a patient responded very well to oral dipyridamole therapy with complete resolution of symptoms and no episodes of ventricular tachycardia at three months. Agents targeting endothelial function are promising; in patients with slow coronary flow, chest pain relief was detected in 90% of patients after nebivolol treatment, and high-sensitive CRP was significantly decreased. Diltiazem has shown benefit as well, with one trial concluding that diltiazem slow-release capsules improved coronary blood flow and alleviated angina in patients with CSF.

## Conclusion

CSFP is a clinically relevant microvascular disorder that should not be dismissed as an incidental angiographic curiosity. As summarised in a recent review, coronary slow flow is an angiographic phenomenon with specific epidemiologic characteristics, associated clinical presentation and prognosis, and it seems appropriate to consider it a distinct disease entity requiring specific treatment. Further research is needed to clarify its pathogenesis and to establish evidence-based therapy.
